stances.claim: The three recent SBN dismissals of Marcos/crony ill-gotten wealth cases are not products of judicial error or bias -- the fault lies squarely with the OSG and PCGG for failing to observe the very basic rules of procedure ('appalling and incredible').

The Benedicto dismissal is correct because affidavits unauthenticated and unidentified by the affiant are hearsay, and the prosecution failed to illustrate the dummy relationship between defendants and Imelda Marcos.

The Tantoco dismissal is correct ('correctly in my humble opinion') because documentary exhibits were excluded for non-presentation during discovery despite SBN and SC directives, and most remaining documents were mere photocopies violating the Best Evidence Rule.

The Gimenez Demurrer to Evidence grant is correct ('correctly in my view') because the Republic's evidence consisted mostly of unauthenticated photocopies with no explanation for the absence of originals; the burden of explaining absence of originals lies on the proponent.

The SC's 2012 Manotoc rebuke -- 'difficult to conceive that one could have finished law school and passed the bar examinations without knowing such elementary rule'... 'deeply disturbing'... 'lawyers of these government agencies are expected to be the best in the legal profession' -- should have been a wake-up call; the 2019 dismissals show it was not heeded.
After cataloguing the procedural failures and the SC's prior rebuke, no further argument is needed -- closing 'Need I say more?' is sufficient indictment.

notable_anecdotes: The opening confession 'I am convinced the fault lies squarely with the OSG and PCGG' -- CJ's most direct attribution of fault to government counsel in the Marcos recovery effort across his columns.

Citation of the SBN's own lament -- 'It saddens the Court that it took more than 30 years before this case (was) submitted for decision and yet, the prosecution failed to present sufficient evidence' -- used as the court's own indictment of the prosecution it presided over.

The technical enumeration of the four authenticators of private documents -- (a) executor, (b) acknowledger, (c) witness, (d) prior-confessor -- recited from the Rules of Court as if to underscore how elementary the failure was.

Excerpting the SC's Manotoc rebuke -- 'difficult to conceive that one could have finished law school and passed the bar examinations without knowing such elementary rule' -- and 'lawyers of these government agencies are expected to be the best in the legal profession' -- as a cumulative shaming.
The closing two-word column-ender 'Need I say more?' -- a rare CJ rhetorical-question closure used when the cited material is so damning that further argument is redundant.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban catalogues three recent SBN dismissals of Marcos/crony ill-gotten wealth cases -- Republic v. Benedicto (Aug 5, 2019, 67 pages, Pahimna ponente), Republic v. Tantoco (Sept 25, 2019, 30 pages, Musngi ponente), and Republic v. Gimenez (Oct 14, 2019, 37 pages, Quiroz ponente) -- and argues that the fault lies squarely with the OSG and PCGG, not the SBN. 'Their failure to observe the very basic rules of procedure is appalling and incredible.' Benedicto fell because affidavits unauthenticated and unidentified by the affiant are hearsay, and the prosecution failed to illustrate the dummy relationship between defendants and Imelda Marcos. Tantoco fell because documents were excluded for non-presentation during discovery 'despite directives of the Court and the Supreme Court' and most of the rest were mere photocopies violating the Best Evidence Rule. Gimenez was a Demurrer to Evidence grant: unauthenticated photocopies disregarded, with no explanation for the absence of originals, and the Rules of Court's four enumerated authenticators of private documents (executor, acknowledger, witness, prior-confessor) ignored. As if lecturing the OSG and PCGG on basic procedures was not enough, the SBN recalled the SC's 2012 rebuke in Republic v. Marcos-Manotoc -- that the best evidence rule has been recognized 'since the 18th century' as one of the most basic rules in law, that 'it is difficult to conceive that one could have finished law school and passed the bar examinations without knowing such elementary rule,' that it is 'deeply disturbing' that 'the very agencies sworn to protect the interest of the state and its people' could conduct prosecution this way, and that 'lawyers of these government agencies are expected to be the best in the legal profession' yet did not even bother to provide any reason for their failure to present originals or witnesses. 'Such manner of legal practice deserves the reproof of this Court.' CJ closes with the silence-as-verdict rhetorical-question: 'Need I say more?'
